## Omics Data Repositories

- Journals and funders now require processed data to be deposited in a repository.
- Many support the deposition of raw data in addition to processed data.
- Gene expression:
  - Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)
  - Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
  - ArrayExpress
- Proteomics
  - Proteomics Identifications (PRIDE)
  - Mass Spectrometry Interactive Virtual Environment (MassIVE)
- Metabolomics
  - MetaboLights
  - Metabolomics Workbench

## Metabolomics Workbench (MW)

- NIH Common Fund's National Metabolomics Data Repository.
- Established in 2012.
- Currently hosts 4261 studies, from 60 countries.
- Organized by:
  - Project: a biological question, contains one or more **related** studies.
  - Study: contains one or more analyses.
  - Analysis: typically one analysis method or sample type, e.g. NMR, MS + chromatography, +ve / -ve mode, etc.
- Our lab has years of experience working with MW data.

## Hypothesis: There Are Significant Numbers of Reusable Datasets in Metabolomics Workbench

- The majority of data within MW is expected to be of good quality.
- Many of the datasets within MW are part of peer-reviewed, published studies.
- Researchers depositing data into MW are trying to do good science.

# Color Grade Evaluation

## Subject Sample Factors (SSF)

- One or more experimentally important metadata about the samples.
  - E.g. Cancerous vs normal, high-fat diet vs normal diet, etc.
- Additional sample data includes things like the raw file name, biological replicate.
- We combine multiple SSF to make a unique label that defines the **experimental groups** of samples.

![](../resources/example_ssf_data.png)

## Number of Samples in Subject Sample Factor Groups

- The number of samples per SSF group indicates if the experimental design is statistically powerful or not, based on general rule of thumb.
- The counts are **after** removing samples with < 10 present metabolites and any outliers.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

  * all SSF groups have $\le$ 2 samples per group ~ [red]{.my-red};
  * 3 $\le$ all SSF groups $\le$ 4 ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow};
  * all SSF groups $\ge$ 5 samples ~ [green]{.my-green};
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| label: n-per-group
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.8
count_nmostcommon_barplot
```

:::

::::


## Using Data Distributions to Define Color Grades

- We can use the full set of datasets themselves to define green (good), yellow (useable), red (double check).



## Percent Missing and Left-Censorship

High percent missingness, especially without the indication of left-censorship; indicates the presence of possible data quality issues.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

* percent missing $\le$ 2 x SD ~ [green]{.my-green} (40.8%);
* 2 x SD $\lt$ percent missing $\le$ 4 x SD limit ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow} (81.7%);
* percent missing $\gt$ 4 x SD limit ~ [red]{.my-red}
* percent missing $\gt$ 10% & lc test p-value $\le$ 0.05 ~ [green]{.my-green};
* percent missing $\gt$ 10% & lc test p-value $\gt$ 0.05 ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow};

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| label: percent-missing-plot
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 4
data_based_cutoffs_plot$pm
```

:::

::::

## Maximum Observed Median Relative Standard Deviation (RSD)

High maximum observed median RSD indicates high variability in the measurements.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

* median RSD $\le$ median of medians + 2 x SD ~ [green]{.my-green} (0.89);
* median of medians + 2 x SD $\lt$ median RSD $\le$ median of medians + 4 x SD ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow} (1.48);
* median RSD $\gt$ median of medians + 4 x SD ~ [red]{.my-red}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| label: max-observed-rsd
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.3
data_based_cutoffs_plot$rsd
```

:::

::::

## Median Within SSF Group Sample-Sample Correlations

Low maximum median within SSF group sample-sample ICI-Kt correlations indicate high biological variance between samples.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

* max median ICI-Kt $\ge$ median of max median - 2 SD ~ [green]{.my-green} (0.54);
* median of max median - 4 SD $\ge$ max median ICI-Kt $\lt$ median of max medians - 2 SD ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow} (0.19);
* max median ICI-Kt $\lt$ median of max medians - 4 SD ~ [red]{.my-red}

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| label: median-cor-plot
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
data_based_cutoffs_plot$med_cor
```

:::

::::

::: footer
RM Flight, PS Bhatt, HNB Moseley, "Information-Content-Informed Kendall-tau Correlation Methodology: Interpreting Missing Values in Metabolomics as Potentially Useful Information" Metabolites 16, 245 (2026).
:::

## Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Scores - PC-90

As more principal components (PC) are needed to account for 90% of the variance in the data (PC-90), it indicates weak signal variance within the dataset in comparison to other sources of variance present.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

  * PC-90 $\le$ median + 2 SD ~ [green]{.my-green} (40); 
  * median + 2 SD $\lt$ PC-90 $\le$ median + 4 SD ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow} (162); 
  * PC-90 $\gt$ median + 4 SD ~ [red]{.my-red}

::: 

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| label: pc-90-plot
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
data_based_cutoffs_plot$pc_90
```

:::

::::

## PCA Scores - ANOVA

Lack of separation of SSF groups across meaningful PCs indicates weak signal variance within the dataset.

Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) p-adjusted: 

  * p-adjust $\le$ 0.05 & PC-perc $\ge$ 5% & factor is SSF or derived ~ [green]{.my-green}; 
  * p-adjust $\le$ 0.05 & PC-perc $\ge$ 5% & factor is additional sample-data or combination of SSF and additional sample-data ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow};
  * p-adjust $\le$ 0.05 & 1% $\le$ PC-perc $\lt$ 5% ~ [yellow]{.my-yellow};
  * p-adjust $\le$ 0.05 & PC-perc $\lt$ 1% ~ [red]{.my-red};
  * p-adjust $\gt$ 0.05 ~ [red]{.my-red}.


::: {.fragment style="position: absolute; bottom: 400px; right: 120px; font-size: 2em; color:black;"}
Mean - median ratio (MMR)
:::

## Detection of Log-Transformed Data


```{r}
#| label: mmr-plot
#| fig-cap: "All plots used datasets with an MMR >= 0.2 and MMR <= 200. **A**: Histogram of Log10(MMR). **B**: Log10(MMR) vs fraction of negative data values, after excluding all datasets with zero negative values. **C**: Histogram of Log10(MMF) for datasets with a maximum observed intensity <= 1000. Vertical lines indicate the MMR cutoffs used of 0.8 (-0.097 on log10 scale) and 1.2 (0.079 on log10 scale) to decide that a dataset should undergo exponentiation."
(mmr_logtransform_plot$mmr_distribution / (mmr_logtransform_plot$mmr_vs_neg | mmr_logtransform_plot$less1000)) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

## Negatives & Missing Values

* MMR and transformation change only a fraction of datasets.
* Negative valuse withough log-transformation should be physically impossible?
* What if we treat negative values as missing?

## Test

$$\text{status} = \begin{cases} 
  \text{green} & \text{if } x \le \tilde{y} \pm 2 \times SD \\
  \text{yellow} & \text{if } \tilde{y} \pm 2 \times SD \lt x \le \tilde{y} \pm 4 \times SD\\
  \text{red} & \text{if } x \gt \tilde{y} \pm 4 \times SD
   \end{cases}
  $$
